game:astraterra-handbook-overview-text:
Astra Terra: Astronomy
The sky over this world is meant to be the real one.

Astra Terra replaces Vintage Story's night sky with a catalog of more than 5,000 stars. Five planets move among them on Keplerian orbits. Nine meteor showers return each year. Four comets return on their own periods; the longest, Halley, about once every seventy-five world years.

The mod gives you the instruments and a blank book. What you write in it is yours. A few prepared books are included in creative, and more are planned as ruin loot.

What you can do
• Watch the sky change with the hour, the season, and how far north or south you have walked.
• Lie on your back with astraterra-liedown so the sky fills the view.
• Form a Sky Disc from clay on your first day, mark sunrises and sunsets, and after a year of marks read the length of the year, your latitude, and when the sun will next stand still.
• Craft a Brass Telescope, put a book in your left hand, and draw constellations.
• Sight a light with the Sextant, write the reading down, and work out whether it stayed put.
• Recover a ruined astrolabe, fit a brass plate, and use the Calibrated Astrolabe to forecast where a recorded figure or a named wanderer will be.

Where to start
Form a Sky Disc from clay and fire it. Mark sunset on the first clear evening. That is astronomy before metal.

When you have brass and glass, craft a telescope. On a dark, cloudless night with open sky, hold a blank book in your left hand, keep ink and quill in your inventory, and draw one constellation.

These pages

Telescopes
The Sky Disc
The Sextant
The Calibrated Astrolabe

Wandering stars
Meteor showers and comets
game:astraterra-handbook-nightsky-text:
Reading the night sky
The same stars, seen from a different place at a different hour, are a different sky.

This is Earth's sky, drawn from a catalog of more than 5,000 stars. It turns with the hour, tilts with your latitude, and shows different figures in different seasons.

How to look
Press astraterra-liedown to lie on your back. In first person the view drops to the grass and looks straight up. Move, jump, or press it again to stand. Every instrument still works while you are lying down. The binding is remappable under Controls as Lie down. Default is Z.

To see stars, draw constellations, or sight anything but the sun and a lit moon, you need a sky dark enough, weather clear enough, and open sky overhead. A telescope still zooms when those conditions fail; the star work does not. The Calibrated Astrolabe predicts rather than observes, so it works in daylight and in bad weather.

Limits
Vintage Story has latitude. It does not have longitude. The sun's hour depends on Z; walking east or west does not change local solar time. On a world whose climate is not set to realistic, latitude is stuck and the sky does not change as you travel. The equator is not at z = 0.

Latitude and the turning of the night
Walk north and the pole star climbs; walk south and it sinks, while stars you have never seen rise ahead of you. Near the poles some figures never set, and others never rise. Every instrument here answers for the latitude you are standing at.

The whole sky wheels around the pole. A constellation low in the east after dusk is high overhead hours later. Its best moment is its transit, when it crosses the meridian at its highest. In the northern hemisphere, Polaris sits near the north celestial pole: it shows north, and its angle above the horizon is your latitude.

The seasons
The stars also rise a little earlier each night, so the sky tells the season as well as the hour. A figure that filled the winter evenings is lost in daylight in summer, and back again a year later.

The Moon
The Moon keeps one surface portrait upright while a curved shadow follows the calendar's phase and turns towards the sun. Vintage Story's moonlight and the length of the night are untouched. A telescope shows a surface rather than a larger smooth disc.
game:astraterra-handbook-telescopes-text:
Telescopes
Glass, brass and a stick, and suddenly there are ten times as many stars.

A telescope zooms the sky. Under magnification, faint smudges resolve into deep-sky objects, planets stop being points of light, and you can draw constellation lines into a book.

How to use it
Hold the Brass Telescope. Hold rightmouse to raise it to your eye. While scoped:
• scroll to change zoom (five steps on the brass telescope).
• middlemouse to cycle modes. The name on the scope is the mode you are in.

Observe looks and zooms only. Nothing in the eyepiece will tell you what a light is. See Wandering stars.
Create Constellation draws: drag with leftmouse from one star you can see to another. Any visible star can start or end a line, not only the named guide stars.
Inspect Constellation names or renames the saved constellation you click.
Remove Segment deletes the segment you click.

Drawing, naming, and removing need a book in your left hand and ink and quill in your inventory. See Constellations and the journal.

The Precision Telescope is the same instrument built around the brass one, with ten stronger zoom steps. Same modes.

Limits
A telescope still zooms when the sky is too bright or too cloudy for astronomy. Drawing and the deep-sky plates need a dark enough, clear enough sky and open sky overhead.
Fifty deep-sky photographs (nebulae, galaxies, clusters) are invisible to the naked eye. Zoom in on a faint smudge.
Raise the glass on a planet and it becomes a disc: Mars swells towards opposition, Saturn carries rings, Jupiter's four Galilean moons and five of Saturn's moons move on their own orbits and vanish when the planet hides them. Put the telescope down and they are points of light again. .stars solar-system photo swaps the pixel-art faces for photographs; position and size stay the same.

The Brass Telescope is plain glass, brass, and a stick (for now).
game:astraterra-handbook-sextant-text:
The Sextant
How high is it? Everything else in navigation starts with that question.

The Sextant measures the altitude of the sun, the moon, a star, a planet, or a comet above the horizon.

How to use it
Hold rightmouse and put the centre of your view on the body. The readout at the top names what you sighted and gives its angle above the horizon in degrees. If several bodies fall in the sight, the one nearest the centre wins.

While holding it, middlemouse cycles the display through the angle alone, the rose equatorial grid, the cyan azimuthal grid, and both together. Letting go restores whatever grid you set with .stars sky-grid; the Sextant remembers its own choice for the rest of the session.

Write the reading down. Hold a writable book in your left hand and keep ink and quill in your inventory. Sneak while sighting. The book gains a dated entry: the angle, the bearing, the brightness, the day and hour, and the latitude you stood at. The entry never says what you sighted, only that something stood there at that hour. Angles are written to one arcminute, which is as fine as this Sextant reads.

Two entries are enough to compare. .stars sightings lays the book out, gathers the entries into the sets it takes to be one body, and says whether each held its place or how fast it moved. .stars classify 2 wanderer Ember is where you say what a set was (set number, then star, wanderer, or comet, then an optional name). Nothing grades the answer. Call a set a wanderer and your own entries are matched against the wandering bodies: if exactly one of them was in all those places on all those nights, your name for it is the name every instrument uses from then on. See Wandering stars.

Limits
The sun and a visibly lit moon can be shot whenever they are up, so the Sextant works in broad daylight. A daytime crescent is a perfectly good sight. An invisible new moon is not offered as a target. Stars and planets need a dark enough sky.
A planet reads as Wandering star unless a book in your left hand names it. Swap books and the sky is renamed at once.
If nothing readable is near the centre the readout tells you what there is to aim at instead, and if the sky above you is blocked it says so.

Sighting the sun costs you nothing here. A real navigator would use a shade glass.
game:astraterra-handbook-skydisc-text:
The Sky Disc
The cheapest instrument here, and the slowest.

The Sky Disc scratches where the sun crosses the horizon. After enough marks, the width of that band gives you the length of the year, how far you are from the equator, where east or west lies, and when the sun will next stand still. One connected constellation can also be cut into the same disc.

How to mark
Stand under open sky as the sun touches the horizon. sneak + hold rightmouse raises the disc and tells you the notch the mark would fall on. Keep holding for about a second and it scratches the rim there. Let go early and nothing is marked. That is the only chance you get to call a scratch off. Come back another evening and mark again. Sunrises go on one rim, sunsets on the other, so either end of the day works.

You are marking the sun crossing the true horizon, not the moment you clicked. A hill in the way costs you nothing, and there is a window either side to get it done. Miss an evening to rain or sleep and nothing is lost: you need enough marks to find the ends of the band, not every day of the year.

How to read it
rightmouse holds the disc up. The readout shows the sunset band, the sunrise band, and, once a rim has turned back from an edge, when the sun will next stand still. scroll turns the raised disc in your hand so you can bring a mark round to the eye.

Two marks bracket a band. Keep marking and the band widens until one evening the mark falls short of the edge. It never went further than that. Around such an evening several days land on the same notch and the sun appears to stand still.

The disc will not tell you a solstice has happened on the day it happens. At the time nobody can know an extreme was one. Only when the band has turned back and reached its far edge does it say anything: then it gives you the length of the year, how far you are from the equator (the width of the band is a function of latitude), and from then on the day the sun will next stand still.

One constellation on the disc
While the disc is held up under the stars, drag with leftmouse from one visible star to another. The line is cut into the disc. No book, ink, or quill. Every later line has to join the figure already there; a line that touches none of it is a second constellation, and there is no room for it.

Hold the finished disc in either hand and its figure returns to the sky. Press a figure into raw clay before you fire it; a fired clay disc will not take another line. Metal can be engraved whenever you like.

Set it down
sneak + rightmouse on the ground puts the disc down face-up, scratches and all. An empty hand and a right click pick it back up. Aim at a block when you mean to place it; aiming at the horizon is how you mark.

Limits
Form a disc on a clay forming surface and fire it in a pit kiln, or craft a copper or bronze one from a metal plate and gold bits. Clay holds a notch of five degrees; metal holds two and a half. They all find the same solstice. A clay rim means more evenings landing on one notch, a sun that appears to stand still for longer, and a year and a latitude handed back rounder. Past copper the rim stops getting better. Every reading says which notch it was read at.

The first mark fixes where the disc belongs. Carry it far enough north or south and it refuses the next mark rather than quietly spoiling the band. A scratch cannot be undone. A rough rim cannot see a small move, so a clay disc wanders further than a metal one before it objects.

Inside the polar circles the sun stops setting for part of the year, and there is no band of sunsets to measure.

Vintage Story's character panel already tells you the day, the month, the year and the hour. .stars calendar clock hides the date and keeps the hour; .stars calendar none hides both and the panel says unreckoned. .stars calendar full puts it back. The choice is local and saved. Until you hide the date, the disc is measuring something the game is already giving you for free.

Why the band knows west
The sun sets due west at the equinoxes and swings evenly either side of that point through the year, so the middle of a finished band of sunsets is due west, at any latitude. The middle of the sunrise band is due east. The disc is never told where north is. A year of evenings is enough.
game:astraterra-handbook-astrolabe-text:
The Calibrated Astrolabe
The telescope shows you what is there. The astrolabe tells you what will be.

The Calibrated Astrolabe forecasts where a constellation, a wanderer you have named, or a comet will stand, and it tells the hour from the sun.

How to get one
Recover a ruined astrolabe from old buildings and combine it with a brass plate.

How to use it
Hold it in your main hand and a written constellation book in your left hand, then hold rightmouse to open the planning readout. The clock still shows if you hold no book.

• middlemouse selects the next target: each constellation in the book, then the wanderers that book has picked out, then the comets.
• scroll forecasts an hour at a time.
• sneak + scroll forecasts seven days at a time.
• sneak + hold rightmouse cuts or recuts the plate for where you are now.

For the selected target it gives the compass direction, the angle above the horizon, whether it is rising or setting, how long until transit, and whether it is circumpolar or can never rise where the plate was cut.

Cutting the plate
An astrolabe is engraved for one latitude. A new one is blank: it reads no plate and will not place a star. Stand under open sky after dusk and hold sneak + rightmouse for a few seconds while it sights the pole. A bar fills as it works. A roof overhead or a sky still too bright will stop it. You need nothing but the sky for this.

Afterwards every position it gives is for that latitude. Travel far enough and it starts reporting how far you have strayed; past about eight degrees it asks to be recut. Until then it is faithfully describing the sky over somewhere else. The clock is not engraved and follows you wherever you go.

Limits
It aims with your book, not with the sky's own catalog. A wandering body nobody has picked out is not on the list at all. Sight one across a few nights, say it wanders, and it appears. Comets are listed whether or not they are here; one that is away reads as the days until it returns. Forecasting that far ahead turns the line into a real position.

Every answer says what it rests on: how many sightings, across how many days, read to what scale, or drawn from N stars, or from the almanac, not your sightings for a comet. An answer with a single night behind it is not allowed to sound like one with a dozen.

Forecasting spans a world year and follows this world's day and year length. A planet is forecast where it will actually be, not where it is now. Let go and the forecast snaps back to the present.

The hour
The astrolabe also tells the time, read off the sun: the hour of the day, whether it is daylight, dusk, night or dawn, the sun's angle above or below the horizon, and how long until the next sunrise or sunset. That clock never drifts, and it follows your forecast, so you can find the hour a constellation stands highest before committing to the wait. Near the poles, where the sun may not rise for a stretch of the year, it says so rather than inventing an hour.
game:astraterra-handbook-constellations-:
Constellations and the journal
A constellation is a line somebody decided to draw. This is the book you draw yours in.

A constellation is a set of lines between stars, stored in a vanilla book or cut into a Sky Disc.

How to draw in a book
Put a blank book in your left hand and keep ink and quill in your inventory. Scope in with a telescope, switch to Create Constellation, and drag from one visible star to another. The segment is written into the book.

Constellations in a book are visible only while you hold that book. Hand it to another player and they see your figures, under your names.

How to cut one into a disc
Hold a Sky Disc up under the stars and drag from star to star. No book and no ink. A disc holds one connected figure. Raw clay takes the figure before firing; fired clay will not. Metal can be engraved later. Hold the disc and the figure returns to the sky.

Limits
Once Astra Terra writes the first constellation into a book, ordinary book editing is locked. The journal keeps working. Ink and quill are needed to create, add to, remove, rename, or build in a book.

Commands
• .stars list: what is in the held book.
• .stars info selected: star and segment counts, the best visibility window, and the current state.
• .stars name, .stars select, .stars delete: manage entries.
• .stars build Ori: write one of the 88 IAU figures straight into the book.

Built figures are ordinary journal entries afterwards: inspect, rename, or delete them like anything you drew by hand. Creative inventory also has a full Star Catalog and The Zodiac.
game:astraterra-handbook-wanderingstars-:
Wandering stars
Five of the lights up there are not stars, and by eye you cannot tell which.

Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn move against the fixed stars. Through a telescope they become discs; to the naked eye they are points of light, same as the stars around them. What gives them away is that they move.

How to work one out
Sight the light with the Sextant on one night and again on another, sneaking each time so a book in your left hand holds two dated entries. Then run .stars sightings to see how far apart those nights put it, and .stars classify 2 wanderer Ember to say what you think it was.

The book takes your word for it. Nothing checks the conclusion against the sky. If your entries pin the conclusion to one wandering body, the book asks what you would like to call it, and every instrument uses that name from then on.

Being wrong is allowed. It shows up later as an instrument forecasting badly from the record you gave it.

Limits
Until a book names it, every instrument calls it a Wandering star. Creative inventory has The Wanderers, which already names all five.

The Calibrated Astrolabe lists a planet only after you have picked it out in the held book. A wanderer nobody has claimed is not on the list at all. Once it is there, it is listed whether or not it is currently up: being told that it is below the horizon and transits in nine hours is the instrument working.

Planets are usually among the brightest things in the sky, which makes them the easiest sights after the sun and the moon.

Why they loop
Chart Mars over a couple of world weeks and it will turn back on itself. Nobody scripted that retrograde loop: it is what the sky does when this world overtakes a slower planet on the inside. A world year is a year of that motion, whatever the world's day count, so Jupiter takes about twelve world years to come back around and Venus swings between the evening and morning sky within a season.
game:astraterra-handbook-cometsandshower:
Meteor showers and comets
The two things in the sky worth staying up for.

Meteor showers return at the same point of every world year, whatever length that year is. Nine of them are in the catalog. A shower is worth watching when its season is near the peak, its radiant is above the horizon, and the sky is dark. A bright moon drowns the faint meteors but not the brightest ones.

Every streak points back toward its shower's radiant. Streaks near that point are short and streaks far across the sky are long, because parallel paths seen in perspective look that way. The strongest shower is the Geminids.

Comets return on their own periods, counted in world years: Machholz about every 5, Tuttle about every 14, Tempel-Tuttle about every 33, and Halley about every 75. Each is the parent of a shower already in the sky, so the dust you watch burn up some nights came off the comet you are waiting for.

How to catch one
Look up during the right season, in the dark, with the radiant above the horizon. The Sextant sights a comet like anything else once it is up. A comet keeps its name without a book: where a planet is a discovery you make by watching, a comet is an event the sky announces.

The Calibrated Astrolabe lists every comet, including the ones that are years away. One that is away reads as the days until it returns. Scroll the forecast that far ahead and the line becomes a real position. .stars comets reports the whole catalog at once.

What an apparition looks like
An apparition lasts a couple of world weeks. The comet moves along its own track against the stars and brightens as it rounds perihelion before fading. For the first nights it is a faint smudge; only near perihelion is it the brightest thing in the sky.

The tail points away from the sun, not along the comet's motion, and swings right around as it passes perihelion. Sunlight and the solar wind push it, so it leans anti-sunward whichever way the comet is going.

You will not wait long for the first. Machholz arrives a little under two world years in. Halley makes its first pass in your third year, and it is the bright one, the only comet here that outshines every star. Its second pass is in world year 78. If you sleep through the first, start a family and impress upon them the importance of looking up.

The periods and the parent showers are real. The tracks across the sky and the peak brightnesses are authored for the game rather than computed from an orbit.
